items.title: Master Microservices: Top 14 Scenario-Based Interview Questions You Need to Know in 2027
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Building reliable software starts with reliable infrastructure.

Synteq is a cloud compute provider built for high availability, with a 99.99% uptime target and its own data centers, racks, hardware, and network.

  • VPS, bare metal, and GPU cloud designed to keep workloads running.

  • Flat monthly bills with no unexpected egress charges.

  • Deploy in minutes using the portal or CLI.

  • Get help directly from engineers, not ticket triage.

If you’re designing systems to survive failures, run them on infrastructure built with availability in mind.

Exclusive to readers of this newsletter: Get your first month FREE!

(Thanks to Synteq for partnering on this newsletter.)

Now let's review some of the key microservices concepts & popular questions that come up in interviews:

1. Asynchronous messaging

“When should microservices talk through a message queue and not call each other directly?”

Use asynchronous messaging when the calling service doesn’t need an immediate response, when tasks take longer to complete, or when services need to handle traffic spikes independently.

For example, checkout publishes an order placed event to a message broker. Payment, email & stock services process the event at their own pace. If one service is down, its messages remain queued until it recovers.

This reduces coupling between services and allows checkout to acknowledge the order without waiting for every downstream service to finish processing.

  • Use when the caller doesn’t need an instant answer--emails or long-running jobs.

  • Queues absorb traffic spikes, so slow consumers could catch up later.

  • One event reaches many consumers through a topic.

  • Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must handle duplicates.

  • Send messages that keep failing to a dead-letter queue for review.

“How do you keep messages in order?”

Most brokers only keep order within one partition.

Send every message for one order to the same partition, using the order ID as the key. Consumers then process each partition one message at a time.

Claiming exactly-once delivery solves duplicates. Across a network, assume at-least-once delivery and make each consumer idempotent.

“A user updates their profile photo, refreshes the page, and still sees the old one. Is this a bug?”

Eventual consistency = copies of data may briefly disagree, but all reach the same value once updates stop.

A write lands on one node and spreads to the others in the background. For a short time window, a read from another node may return the old value. The system stays up and fast even when some nodes can’t talk.

Within milliseconds or seconds, every copy catches up.

  • Explain the cause: write landed on one copy but the read hit another.

  • It’s fine for feeds, likes, and catalogs.

  • Fix the user’s own view with read-your-writes, such as reading from the primary for a short time after a write.

  • Keep strong consistency for money & stock.

“Two users edit the same record on different nodes at once. Which change wins?”

You need a conflict rule.

Last write wins is simple but can lose an update. Version numbers let you spot the conflict and reject the stale write. Some systems merge both changes automatically.

Treating eventual consistency as NO consistency.

Copies are guaranteed to converge. Strong candidates also say how long “eventually” takes in their system and how they’d measure it.

3. Timeouts and retries with backoff

“A downstream call fails now and then. How do you make the caller more reliable?”

Timeouts and retries with backoff define how long a caller waits and when it retries.

A timeout ends the wait after a set time, so threads don’t pile up. A retry then repeats the call for brief failures, like a dropped packet. Backoff doubles the wait before each new attempt.

Jitter adds a random offset, so thousands of clients don’t retry at the same instant.

  • Always set a timeout slightly above the call’s normal slowest response time.

  • Retry only brief errors, like timeouts or a , never a .

  • Use exponential backoff with jitter.

  • Cap the number of retries.

  • Retry only idempotent operations.

“Service A call B, B call C, and each one retries three times.

What happens when C fails?”

The retries multiply. One user request can turn into nine calls to C, and more with each extra layer. A small failure becomes a flood. Retry at one layer only, usually the outer one, and let the inner layers fail fast.

Retrying in a tight loop without a limit. A short outage then turns into a retry storm.

“When would you choose gRPC over REST?”

A remote procedure call () lets one service call a function on another service as if it were local.

You define the service and its messages in a contract file. A tool generates client and server code from it. gRPC sends compact binary messages using Protocol Buffers. It runs over HTTP/2, which carries many calls on one connection at once.

  • Choose gRPC for frequent calls between internal services.

  • Binary messages are smaller & faster to parse than JSON.

  • Typed contracts with generated code catch mismatches at build time.

  • HTTP/2 supports streaming in both directions.

  • Keep REST for public APIs & browsers, as browsers need a proxy for gRPC.

“How do you change a gRPC contract without breaking callers?”

Add new fields with new field numbers. Never reuse or change an existing number. Mark removed fields as reserved. Old clients simply ignore fields they don’t know.

Treating a remote call like a local one. It can timeout, fail, or run slow, so you still need timeouts & retries.

5. Distributed transaction

“Bob sends ten dollars to Alice. But their accounts live in different databases.

How do you keep the money correct?”

Use a distributed transaction to coordinate the debit from Bob’s account and the credit to Alice’s account across both databases.

If one operation fails, the system must either roll back the transaction or recover through retries or compensating actions.

Patterns like two-phase commit (), Saga, and Try-Confirm-Cancel () achieve this with different consistency and availability trade-offs.

Each transfer should also have a unique transaction ID to prevent duplicate debits or credits during retries.

  • Explain the failure first: money leaves Bob’s account but never reaches Alice’s.

  • Name the options: two-phase commit, try-confirm-cancel, and saga.

  • Pick based on needs: strict consistency or availability & scale.

  • Ask whether the data could live in one service, which removes the problem.

  • Give each transfer an ID and a state, and make every step idempotent.

“Which approach would you pick for a payments system?”

A saga or try-confirm-cancel, with a durable record of each transfer.

Every step is idempotent, so retries are safe. A reconciliation job checks balances against the ledger and flags anything that doesn’t match.

Jumping straight to a pattern name without explaining the crash case. Interviewers want to hear what goes wrong before you fix it.

6. Independent deployability

“How do you release a change to one service without breaking services which call it?”

Make each service independently deployable by giving it its own build & deployment pipeline and maintaining backward-compatible API contracts.

Use to verify that changes don’t break existing callers. If a breaking change is unavoidable, introduce a new API version and keep the old version running until all callers migrate.

Use or deployments to release changes gradually & roll back if something goes wrong.

This allows each service to evolve and deploy independently without requiring coordinated releases.

  • Make changes backward compatible. Add fields, and never remove/rename them in one step.

  • Version the API when a breaking change cannot be avoided & run both versions side by side.

  • Run contract tests in each pipeline, so a provider can’t break what its consumers expect.

  • Release safely with canary or blue-green deployments and a fast rollback.

“Every caller uses a field you need to rename. How do you do it?”

Use expand and contract. Add the new field next to the old one, and return both. Move callers to the new field one at a time. Once nobody reads the old field, remove it.

Relying on a shared test environment and a joint release of several services. If services must ship together, you’ve built a distributed monolith. Interviewers listen for whether you know the term.

“Your mobile app makes 8 API calls to load one screen. How do you fix it?”

Use the Backend for Frontend () pattern to replace many API calls with a single call from the mobile app.

BFF gives each client type its own gateway, shaped around what the client needs.

The BFF calls the required backend services in parallel where possible, combines their responses, and returns only the data the mobile screen needs. You can also create a separate BFF for the web application, as it may have different data requirements.

This reduces network round trips, minimizes payload size & simplifies client-side logic.

  • Name the pattern: a backend built for one client experience.

  • BFF calls the services in parallel and returns one response sized for the screen.

  • It trims fields for mobile to save data and battery life.

  • The engineers who build the app also own its BFF, so both change together.

  • Mention GraphQL as an option, as it lets the client ask for exact fields it needs.

“You have web, iOS, and Android apps. One BFF or three?”

One per experience, not one per platform. iOS and Android share screens, so one mobile BFF serves both. Web gets its own.

Split further only when the needs truly differ.

Letting business rules creep into each BFF. The same pricing rule then lives in three places and drifts apart. A BFF should shape data, not make business decisions.

“One slow downstream service is taking down your whole service.

Why and how do you stop it?”

A slow downstream service can exhaust shared resources, such as threads or connections, leaving no resources available to communicate with healthy services.

Use the Bulkhead pattern to isolate resources by giving each downstream service its own thread pool and/or concurrency limit.

If one downstream service becomes slow or unresponsive, it exhausts only its allocated resources while other services continue to operate normally.

Combine bulkheads with timeouts to release blocked resources & prevent cascading failures.

  • Explain the cause: slow calls hold every thread in a shared pool.

  • Give each downstream service its own pool or concurrency limit.

  • Combine bulkheads with timeouts, so stuck threads free up.

  • Apply the same idea at a larger scale--separate clusters for critical traffic.

“How big should each pool be?”

Work it out from load tests. Calls per second times normal response time gives the number of calls in flight at once. Add some headroom, then cap it. Watch rejected calls in production and then fine-tune.

Only adding more threads. A bigger shared pool delays the failure but doesn’t stop it.

“Instances of your service start and stop all day.

How do other services know where to send requests?”

Use a service registry to maintain an up-to-date list of running service instances and their network addresses.

When an instance starts, it registers its address with the registry. When it shuts down, it deregisters itself. Regular health checks help identify and remove unhealthy instances. Other services query the registry to discover available instances and send requests to them.

This allows service instances to start, stop, and move between machines without requiring callers to update hard-coded addresses.

  • Describe the registry as a directory of live instances and their addresses.

  • Name both styles: self-registration and third-party registration.

  • Health checks or heartbeats remove dead instances.

  • The registry must stay up, so run it as a cluster with replicated data.

  • Callers cache the instance list, so they keep working through short registry outages.

“What happens if the registry goes down?”

Callers keep using their cached instance lists, so existing traffic still flows. But new instances can’t register, and dead ones aren’t removed. The caches slowly go stale. Running three or five registry nodes means one failure doesn’t stop lookups.

Hard-coding addresses, or using DNS records with long cache times. Containers move and addresses change, so stale entries send traffic to dead instances.

“How does two-phase commit work, and why do microservices usually avoid it?”

Two-phase commit () is a protocol where a coordinator gets every database to agree before any of them commits.

In the , the coordinator asks each participant to get ready. Each one writes the change to disk, locks the rows, and votes yes/no.

In the , the coordinator counts the votes. All yes means commit everywhere. Any no, or any timeout, means roll back everywhere.

  • Walk through both phases: prepare and vote, then commit or rollback.

  • It gives all-or-nothing results across databases.

  • Participants hold locks through both phases, which slows everything down.

  • Many modern databases and brokers don’t support XA transactions.

  • It still works well within one trusted system.

“The coordinator crashes after everyone votes yes. What happens?”

The participants are stuck. They can’t commit or roll back on their own, so they hold their locks until the coordinator recovers and reads its log.

This blocking is 2PC's main weakness.

Saying 2PC keeps the system both consistent and available. It gives up availability to stay consistent.

11. Configuration manager

“How do you change a setting across 200 services without redeploying them?”

Use a centralized configuration manager to store & update settings for all 200 services.

Each service loads its configuration at startup and either watches for changes or periodically checks the configuration store for updates.

When you change a setting, such as a feature flag or log level, the services reload the updated value at runtime without requiring a redeployment. Also keep configuration changes versioned, so you can quickly roll back if something goes wrong.

Note: some settings may still require a service restart.

  • Use one central store, with values per environment and full version history.

  • Services read settings at startup and reload them when they change.

  • Control who can view or edit each value, per service and per environment.

  • Keep secrets like passwords in a separate vault, encrypted & rotated.

  • Roll out risky changes to a few instances first through feature flags.

“A bad config value took down production. How do you prevent a repeat?”

Check every value against a schema before it goes live. Roll changes out to a small group of instances first. Keep version history, so you can roll back in seconds. Treat config changes like code, with review and an audit log.

Storing passwords and API keys with ordinary settings, or committing them to git. Interviewers expect you to keep secrets separate.

“Your startup’s founder wants to launch with 20 microservices. What do you say?”

Monolith first. You start a new product as a well-structured monolith and split it into services only when complexity demands it.

A new product changes shape every few weeks. Splitting it into services too early locks in boundaries you’ll soon regret. A modular monolith keeps clean internal modules inside one deployable unit.

Once a module grows stable and busy, you extract it into its own service.

  • Push back with reasons: domain is still unknown, boundaries will move, and 20 services need costly tooling.

  • Propose a modular monolith with enforced module boundaries.

  • Agree on the signals for extracting a service: scale, release speed, or group ownership.

  • Name the strangler fig pattern: route traffic for one feature to a new service and retire the old code bit by bit.

“How do you stop a modular monolith from turning into a tangled mess?”

Enforce boundaries in code.

Each module exposes a public interface, and other modules can’t touch its internals. Tools like ArchUnit or Spring Modulith fail the build when a module breaks the rules.

Each module also owns its own tables, with no joins across modules.

Treating monolith first as “monolith forever.” It’s a starting point with a plan to extract services later. Without enforced boundaries, the plan never happens.

“How would you book a hotel room and a flight so the customer gets both or neither?”

Try-confirm-cancel () is a pattern where each service first reserves resources, then confirms or releases them.

In the try step, each service checks and holds what it needs. If every try succeeds, each service runs confirm and makes the change final. If any try fails, each service runs cancel and releases its hold.

Each service writes its own try, confirm, and cancel code.

  • Try holds the room and the seat. Confirm books them. Cancel releases them.

  • Holds are business records, so no database locks remain open between steps.

  • A coordinator decides whether to confirm or cancel.

  • Holds expire after a timeout, so a crash doesn’t block stock forever.

  • Make confirm and cancel idempotent since the coordinator will retry them.

“How is TCC different from a saga?”

TCC holds first and commits later, so nothing is final until confirm. A saga commits each step at once and undoes it if a later step fails.

TCC keeps other requests from seeing half-done work. A saga suits longer workflows.

Saying TCC needs no coordinator. Something has to decide to confirm or cancel for every part. Frameworks like Apache Seata run the coordinator for you.

“How should you organize engineers around microservices?”

Conway’s law says that a system’s design mirrors the communication structure of the organization building it.

Put three groups of engineers on one compiler, and you get a three-pass compiler. Services follow the same rule. If two groups share one service, its code splits along their lines.

If one group owns five services, those services tend to blur together.

  • One group owns each service from design to production.

  • Group boundaries should match service boundaries, or the code will drift toward the org chart.

  • Avoid shared ownership. A service with two owners has no real owner.

  • Mention the inverse Conway maneuver: shape the groups first to get the architecture you want.

“What happens to the services after a reorganisation?”

The services keep their old boundaries while the groups change.

Ownership blurs & changes slow down. Give every service one clear owner, record it in a service catalog, and plan to merge or split services that no longer fit.

Treating Conway’s law as trivia. Interviewers want you to link it to design, such as why a shared service with five owning groups becomes slow to change.

Every question in this guide tests one skill: explaining tradeoffs out loud.

Three habits will sharpen every answer:

  • Explain the failure first. Say what breaks before you name the pattern that fixes it.

  • Every pattern adds delay, code, or extra parts. Say which ones.

  • Answer the follow-up early. Mention the edge case, such as a failed refund or a stale cache, before the interviewer asks.

Pick questions from these guides (here’s part 1), and set a timer for three minutes each. Answer them out loud, and record yourself. Listen back for the vague parts and fix those first.

items.title: How to Build an AI Code Assistant
items.author: Louis-François Bouchard
items.content:
A code assistant looks like one product:

You type & it completes your line.

You ask a question & it answers from your codebase.

You describe a change & it edits the files.

Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex all present these as a single experience.

Yet under the surface, they’re 3 separate systems with almost nothing in common.

  • Autocomplete has 300 milliseconds to return a suggestion before the developer types past it. It runs a small, fast model on a narrow window of local context, and speed matters most.

  • Chat has seconds, not milliseconds, but it has to find and read the right files in a codebase it has never seen.

  • Agent mode has minutes, but it writes code, runs it, and must recover when tests fail.

Each mode uses a different model, context strategy & evaluation.

The constraint on autocomplete is latency… While the constraint for chat is knowledge… And for agent, the constraint is trust.

This newsletter designs all three modes, then builds the local core from scratch.

Please--whatever you do--don’t assume your AI-generated code is secure because it works and passes tests. Everything is not OK.

If you believe what the experts say, mark my words-the only thing the rise of AI coding agents is going to do is split engineering teams into two separate and yet highly unequal groups:

The haves and the have-nots… those who adapt their security practices, actively hunt for exploitable vulnerabilities, and fix weaknesses before attackers exploit them...and those who fail to recognize the growing security risks, complacently shipping AI-generated code.

So which side will you end up on?

  • Reviews every pull request for security vulnerabilities before code gets merged.

  • Uses AI-powered security analysis to hunt for potentially exploitable vulnerabilities across your codebase.

  • Maps entry points, trust boundaries, and security-sensitive operations to show what got verified and what needs attention.

  • Vulnerability Verification: Checks findings for reachability, existing safeguards, and exploitation conditions to filter unsupported findings.

  • Drafts fixes as pull requests for developers to review, test, and approve.

  • Evaluates how code changes affect downstream services and security boundaries.

  • Tracks security findings as code changes, showing what got verified and what still needs attention.

  • Traces potential security risks across linked repositories and services.

When you start your 14-day free trial, you will get access to CodeRabbit Secure. It’ll help you find, verify, and fix security vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.

Get one FREE Deep Scan when you try CodeRabbit Secure. Use it to uncover potential security vulnerabilities hiding in your codebase.

(Thanks to CodeRabbit for partnering on this newsletter.)

The full design covers repo exploration, multi-model routing, tool use, source code privacy, and optional RAG over code, with autocomplete held to a few hundred milliseconds budget.

The companion build implements the working core of that design: repository chat and exploration, approval-gated file edits, read-only commands, model routing, a callable FIM completion path, and optional semantic RAG.

Many of these terms might be new if you have not worked on code tooling before, but don’t worry, each one is explained where it first appears…

He’s a best-selling author (Building LLMs for Production), the co-founder of Towards AI, and the creator of the YouTube channel What’s AI, where he helps people understand AI and learn how to apply it in the real world. Through his development work with clients, content, teaching, AI training programs, and the new Mentorship program at Towards AI Academy, Louis focuses on making AI practical for builders, engineers, and curious learners alike.

At Towards AI, he and his team train AI engineers through courses and mentorship built for every stage, from beginner to advanced. That educational mission, plus the real-world experience of building for his clients, is exactly why I wanted him in this newsletter series.

Here’s what’s inside this newsletter:

  • Your AI coding assistant could know your entire codebase and still give the wrong answer. The hidden limitations of code search, and why finding the right function becomes harder as your repository grows.

  • Your fastest AI model could make your coding assistant painfully slow. Autocomplete has a strict latency target, while chat and agent tasks need different capabilities. The surprising trade-offs behind choosing the right models.

  • Your AI agent could fix one bug and create three more. Giving an AI permission to read files, execute commands, and modify code introduces risks that a working prototype might never reveal.

  • A 7B coding model passed 3 out of 5 edit tasks. A 32B model passed 3 out of 3. The small benchmark that raises a bigger question about model size, tool reliability, and when paying for a stronger model makes sense.

  • Your AI coding assistant could pass every demo and still fail in production. The gaps between a laptop prototype and a production system, and what changes when many developers start trusting AI agents with their code.

Why Build Your Own Code Assistant?

GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf & Claude Code already work well for most developers.

For individual use, choosing an existing tool makes more sense.

Yet there are two good reasons to build your own:

Building each mode yourself helps you understand how AI code assistants work.

You learn why autocomplete feels instant, how much context and how many tool calls an assistant needs to understand your codebase, and why agents sometimes make incorrect/unnecessarily broad changes.

Building your own assistant makes sense when existing tools cannot meet your engineering requirements.

  • Your codebase has unique context. Public models have never seen your internal frameworks, naming conventions, or service boundaries. An assistant that understands your wrapper and error-handling patterns provides more relevant help than one that only knows generic Python.

  • Your source code must stay within your infrastructure. Many hosted assistants offer enterprise data controls and zero-retention options. Yet strict security requirements in regulated industries, defense, or environments with sensitive intellectual property sometimes prohibit code from leaving your infrastructure. Local or self-hosted inference addresses this requirement.

  • You need control over latency. Autocomplete must respond almost instantly. A local model avoids network round trips, while a self-hosted model keeps requests within your network. Provider-side caching reduces processing time, but network latency remains. Owning the endpoint gives you more control over response times.

  • General models struggle with domain-specific languages (DSLs). Proprietary scripting languages, SQL dialects, infrastructure-as-code files, and internal APIs receive limited coverage in public training data. Fine-tuning or prompting a model with relevant examples could improve performance, provided you have suitable training data and evaluations.

  • High request volume increases costs. Autocomplete runs whenever developers pause while typing. Across an engineering team, these requests add up quickly. A small, inexpensive model handles autocomplete, while a larger model handles complex chat and agent tasks. This approach helps control inference costs.

For individual developers, an existing assistant is usually the practical choice.

Building one yourself is valuable when you want to understand how its different modes work. For engineering teams, building a custom assistant makes sense when specific requirements justify owning the infrastructure.

The AI code assistant has three modes: autocomplete, chat, and agent.

They appear as one product to the developer, but each serves a different purpose and has unique technical requirements.

The practical build implements a simplified local version.

I’ll explain where the full production design includes additional features.

Three Modes, Three Requirements

  • Returns code suggestions within 300 milliseconds for at least half of requests (p50). The p95 latency measures the time within which 95% of requests finish.

  • Answers questions about files, functions, symbols, and repository structure, with references to relevant file paths and line numbers.

  • Reads and edits files, executes approved commands, and, in the full design, runs tests to detect errors and improve its changes.

The practical build supports file exploration, read-only commands, and edits that require approval. It does not execute tests.

All three modes use common code exploration tools:

  • , , locate relevant files and code.

  • Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) lookup: Finds functions and classes by examining the structure of the code.

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Adds embedding-based code search when repositories become too large for basic exploration.

A sends complex chat and agent requests to a larger model and simpler requests to a smaller model.

Autocomplete uses its dedicated Fill-in-the-Middle () model directly to minimize latency.

In the full design, agents execute commands inside isolated containers and request approval for sensitive actions.

The practical build runs locally on Ollama. It restricts commands through an allowlist, blocks access to sensitive files and paths outside the workspace, and requires approval before writing changes. A self-hosted deployment is also an option for engineering teams.

Agent mode proposes code changes as diffs, letting developers review modifications before applying them.

The practical build lets you accept/reject changes in the terminal.

The full design adds an editor interface where you can review and modify proposed changes. It also separates the frontend, AI models, exploration tools, and sandboxed workspace.

Why Autocomplete Is Different

Autocomplete has the strictest latency requirements.

Chat and agent requests have seconds or minutes to complete. Autocomplete targets roughly 300 milliseconds before the developer resumes typing.

This tight deadline determines which model to use, how much context to collect, and which processing steps to skip.

Part 1: Autocomplete and 300ms Budget

Autocomplete is the feature developers use most and notice least.

It fires on every pause in typing, suggests the rest of a line or block, and the developer either accepts/types past it. GitHub describes code completion as its most widely used Copilot feature. Everything about how it is built follows from one fact: a suggestion that arrives late is never shown, and a suggestion that is never shown has an acceptance rate of zero regardless of quality.

A fast, decent suggestion beats a slow, smart one every time.

In practice, means well under a second.

The best systems aim for a few hundred milliseconds. Typing rhythm sets the target: suggestions must appear during the pause before the developer resumes, and the acceptance rate drops as latency increases.

The engineering team behind Cody, Sourcegraph’s AI coding assistant, drove single-line completion from a 75th-percentile latency of 1.8 seconds to under 900 milliseconds, treating anything past a second as too slow.

This newsletter sets a stricter working target of roughly 300ms for the median request.

Treat it as an illustrative design target, not an industry standard. This is plausible with a small local model & fast serving, with no network round trip to pay for, but whether a given 1 to 3B model reaches it on specific hardware is a question only measurement answers.

The 300 milliseconds are not spent in one place.

Instead, they’re split across five stages, each competing for the same window:

  • is the wait after the last keystroke before firing a request, typically a few tens of milliseconds, so the system does not fire on every character.

  • gathers the code around the cursor & nearby signals.

  • converts that context into tokens.

  • is the model’s prefill latency & is usually the cost.

  • delivers the suggestion token by token.

The model owns only part of the budget.

If debounce & context assembly take 80ms, the model has roughly 220ms left to produce a usable suggestion. Context assembly competes directly with inference for the remaining time, which means the editor has to be deliberate about how much context it gathers.

The editor sends a small amount of relevant code (instead of the entire repository) to the AI model.

  • The lines immediately before & after where you’re typing.

  • Other files you’re currently working with.

  • Code you’ve recently modified.

  • Related modules and dependencies.

The editor selects the most relevant snippets because larger prompts require more processing time, thus increasing time-to-first-token ().

Sourcegraph’s Cody ranks recently viewed files and open tabs by their similarity to the code around the cursor. GitHub Copilot also uses the current file and related workspace files to build context.

Both approaches prioritize to keep autocomplete fast.

Chat mode faces a larger context-selection problem because it searches across the repository. (We’ll explore this in Part 2.)

For autocomplete, the next step is to generate code that fits the cursor’s position.

Traditional chat models generate text by predicting what comes next.

Yet code autocomplete has a different requirement: the generated code must fit between existing lines.

Fill-in-the-Middle () solves this by dividing the code into three parts:

  • Existing code before the cursor.

  • Existing code after the cursor.

  • New code the model generates between them.

Imagine the function below the cursor returns a object.

A model that reads only the prefix must guess what comes next. An FIM model also reads the suffix, thus generating code consistent with the function’s return type.

GitHub encountered problems when using ordinary chat models for code completion. Suggestions sometimes appeared in the wrong location, repeated existing code, or overwrote subsequent lines.

Although prompting a chat model with the suffix approximates this behavior, FIM-trained models are better suited to reliable inline completion.

Models such as Qwen2.5-Coder and FIM-capable variants of Code Llama and DeepSeek Coder use special tokens to identify the three parts.

The general prompt structure looks like this:

<PRE>{prefix}<SUF>{suffix}<MID>

Each model family uses its own token format.

  • for the prefix.

  • for the suffix.

  • to begin generation.

(The practical build in Part 6 uses Qwen’s FIM format.)

Model variants differ in their FIM support, so selecting a compatible model matters.

The next challenge is producing it fast enough for autocomplete…

Speculative Decoding and Prefix Caching

Here are 2 techniques to reduce autocomplete latency without changing the model’s output quality.

A small draft model predicts several tokens ahead. A larger target model then verifies them in a single forward pass.

When the predictions are correct, the system accepts multiple tokens at once instead of generating them one by one.

This speeds up generation while preserving the target model’s output distribution.

The code above the cursor usually changes very little between keystrokes.

Prefix caching reuses the Key-Value () cache from earlier requests instead of processing the same context again.

This reduces repeated computation, especially when the prompt contains thousands of tokens.

Yet there’s a limitation: FIM places the suffix after the prefix in the token sequence. So reusing the suffix’s cache requires additional support from the inference server.

Both techniques help reduce latency. Prefix caching reduces prompt processing time, while speculative decoding accelerates token generation.

But faster inference raises another question: how large should the autocomplete model be?

A small, fast model is better for autocomplete than a larger, slower one.

  • Produces simple completions quickly & consistently.

  • Handles harder completions more accurately but could exceed the latency budget.

If the larger model misses the response deadline on a third of requests, its additional accuracy becomes less useful.

Plus, the hardware matters. A 7B model would respond fast enough on a server GPU, while a smaller model is more practical on a laptop.

Autocomplete typically handles short, predictable tasks:

  • Complete a function argument.

A small FIM model handles these common cases without the overhead of a larger model.

Speculative decoding and prefix caching could make larger models practical in some deployments. Yet the default autocomplete path favors a small, dedicated model, as we’ll discuss in Part 4.

Sourcegraph reported lower latency and higher suggestion acceptance after moving Cody’s fast path to a smaller, code-specific model.

But acceptance alone does not tell you whether the suggestions are useful.

The best autocomplete model produces suggestions developers actually keep.

Here are two metrics to measure this:

  • The percentage of suggestions developers accept.

  • How much of an accepted suggestion remains in the code after subsequent edits.

But acceptance rate alone can be misleading.

For example, a model that frequently suggests short, obvious completions could achieve a high acceptance rate without providing much value.

GitHub encountered this problem and introduced accepted and retained characters, which measure how much suggested code survives over time.

Sourcegraph’s Cody uses edit distance to track a similar signal.

Consider a suggestion that a developer accepts but immediately rewrites. The acceptance rate counts it as successful, even though it provided limited value.

Retention helps reveal these cases.

The metrics you optimize influence which model you deploy. (Part 5 covers the evaluation scorecard across autocomplete, chat, and agent modes.)

Autocomplete operates under a strict 300-millisecond latency target. Every design choice must account for this constraint.

Chat mode has a different challenge. When you ask a question about your codebase, the assistant needs enough repository context to provide an accurate answer.

When you upgrade, you’ll get:

  • Simple breakdown of real-world architectures

  • Frameworks you can plug into your work or business

  • Proven systems behind ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Copilot

items.title: Top 13 Microservices Interview Questions Answered
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Last year, I met a young software engineer who walked into an interview, confident he knew the fundamentals.

But he struggled to answer some simple questions about microservices.

His story is why I wrote this letter.

  • Design your system architecture in Miro

  • Document API, database & caching decisions

  • Connect Claude Code through Miro’s MCP server

  • Retrieve the architecture context from the Miro board

  • Generate an implementation plan based on that context

  • Bring the plan back to Miro for team review

I tried this workflow with a URL shortener architecture & it saved me hours of work.

It lets your coding agent work with existing architecture decisions, so you can spend less time repeating context and more time building.

(Thanks to Miro for partnering on this newsletter.)

Here are the top 13 must-know interview questions with answers:

“What problems do microservices solve & what new problems do they create?”

Microservices split one application into small services, each running in its own process and deployed independently.

An online shop might run separate services for catalog, cart, payments, and shipping. Each has its own code, data, and release schedule. Services talk over the network through application programming interfaces ().

A small group of engineers owns each service from design to production.

  • They solve coordination problems. Each group ships its own service without waiting for a shared release.

  • Also they let you scale each service independently. A busy search service gets more instances while the rest stay small.

  • Yet they create network problems. Every call can be slow, fail, or arrive twice.

  • Plus, they create data problems. No single database transaction spans services, so you need sagas or eventual consistency.

  • And they need tooling before the first service goes live: service discovery, tracing, and automated deployment.

“How do you decide where to draw the line between two services?”

Split along business capabilities, such as payments/shipping, not technical layers.

Each service should own its data and change for one business reason. If two services always deploy “together or call each other” on every request, they belong in one service.

Listing only the benefits.

This question tests whether you know the costs. “Microservices are more scalable” with no mention of network failures or split data sounds like you’ve only read about them.

Strong candidates also say when not to use them, such as a small product with a handful of engineers.

“What’s the difference between an API gateway & a load balancer?”

An API gateway is a single entry point that receives every client request and routes it to the right service.

The gateway handles the work every request needs. It checks the token, applies rate limits, and validates the request. Then it finds the target service and forwards the call.

It also merges several service responses into one reply for the client.

  • A load balancer spreads traffic across copies of one service.

  • While a gateway reads paths, headers, and tokens, then decides which service gets the request.

  • They work together. A load balancer sits in front of several gateway instances.

“Your gateway is becoming a bottleneck. What do you do?”

Keep the gateway stateless and run more instances behind the load balancer.

Cache token checks. Move heavy work like response merging into “backend for frontend”. If it’s still too much, split the gateway by domain.

Putting business rules in the gateway, such as discount logic.

The gateway then changes with every feature and needs every group’s sign-off, which recreates the enterprise service bus problem.

“Compare client-side and server-side service discovery.”

Service discovery is how a caller finds a healthy instance of the service it wants to reach.

In discovery, the caller queries the registry itself. It gets a list of instances and picks one.

In discovery, the caller sends the request to a router/gateway. The router then queries the registry and forwards the call.

  • Client-side: one less network hop & callers can pick smarter routes.

  • But client-side needs a discovery library in every language you use.

  • Server-side: callers stay simple as the router does the lookup.

  • Yet the router adds an extra hop and must keep its address cache in sync.

“Which would you use on Kubernetes?”

Server-side, since it’s built in.

Each Service gets a stable DNS name, and the platform routes to healthy pods. A client-side library adds little there. If you need smarter routing, a service mesh adds it without code changes.

Mixing up the registry and discovery.

The registry stores where instances live… Discovery is how a caller uses it.

Treating them as one thing makes the answer vague.

“Order service needs customer details stored in customer database. How does it get them?”

Database per service means each service owns its data store, and other services reach data only through the owner’s API.

Order service owns the orders database. If shipping needs order details, it calls the order API or listens for order events. Each service can also pick the store that suits it best.

Search might use Elasticsearch while payments stays on PostgreSQL.

  • Never read another service’s tables directly!

  • Instead, call the customer API when you need fresh data.

  • Or keep a local read copy, updated from customer events for speed & resilience.

  • Tradeoff: API call is fresh but adds a runtime dependency, while a local copy is fast but slightly stale.

  • For reports across services, feed a separate read store from events.

“How do you make sure the event goes out whenever the data changes?”

Use the transactional outbox pattern:

Write the change and the event into the same local transaction, with the event in an outbox table. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes each event.

This avoids a commit that succeeds while the publish fails.

Saying services could share one database as long as each uses its own tables. A shared database still schema changes, load, and outages across services.

“A customer places an order. You need to reserve stock, charge the card, and book delivery. Yet each step lives on a different service. How do you keep data correct?”

A saga splits one long transaction into a chain of local transactions, each with an undo step called a “compensating transaction".

An order saga might reserve stock, charge the card, and book delivery. Each step commits in its own service right away. If delivery booking fails, the saga runs compensations in reverse.

It refunds the card & releases the stock.

  • Explain why one database transaction cannot span three services.

  • Explain why two-phase commit is a poor fit: long locks across services hurt availability.

  • Walk through the saga: each step commits locally, each has a compensating step.

  • Name both styles of Saga. In “choreography”, services react to each other’s events. In “orchestration”, one orchestrator tells each service what to do next.

“What happens if the refund itself fails?”

Retry the compensation until it succeeds; every compensation must be idempotent. Plus, store the saga’s state, so a crash can resume from the last step.

If retries keep failing, raise an alert for manual handling.

Saying a saga keeps data consistent at every moment.

Other requests can see half-finished states between steps. Strong candidates say how they’d handle this, such as marking the order “pending” until the saga completes.

“Your order service calls a payment service. Payment starts timing out. What happens to the order service, and how do you protect it?”

A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service once errors cross a threshold, then lets a few test calls through later.

The breaker starts closed and calls flow normally. When failures pass a set rate, it trips open. Every call now fails fast without touching the broken service. After a cooldown, it moves to half-open and allows a few test calls.

Success closes it again, but failure opens it again.

  • Threads in the order service wait on slow payment calls, pile up, and the order service fails as well.

  • A circuit breaker trips once the failure rate crosses a threshold, so calls fail fast.

  • Name the three states: closed, open, and half-open.

  • Pair the breaker with a timeout and a fallback. On its own, it only turns slow errors into fast ones.

“How do you pick the threshold?”

Start from real traffic data.

Use a failure rate over a sliding window, not a raw error count, so quiet periods don’t trip it. Set a minimum number of calls before it can trip. Then tune it from what you see in production.

Describing the breaker as a retry mechanism. Retries keep calling the broken service. A breaker stops calling it.

“You’re starting a new product with 5 engineers. Would you build a monolith or microservices?”

A monolith is one application where every module ships together as a single deployable unit.

Orders, payments, and user accounts live in one codebase. They share one process and usually one database. Modules talk through plain function calls, so each call is fast and fails loudly.

You build it once, test it once, and deploy it once.

  • Pick a monolith first. Five engineers ship faster with one codebase, one pipeline, and one deploy.

  • The product will change shape often, so service boundaries drawn now will probably be wrong.

  • Keep clean module boundaries inside the monolith. Each module owns its own tables, and other modules call it through a clear interface.

  • Name the signals for splitting later: builds get slow, engineers block each other’s releases, or one module needs to scale on its own.

“Your monolith has grown to 60 engineers. What do you do?”

Find the module with the most pain first, such as the one that changes most often or needs to scale most.

Extract it into its own service behind the same interface. Route traffic to the new service bit by bit, and keep the old code path until the new one proves stable.

Repeat one module at a time, never all at once.

Calling the monolith outdated by default.

Interviewers want to hear you match the architecture to the size of the group and the product. A rewrite into many services on day one is the answer they’re testing you against.

Shopify still runs a very large Rails monolith, so “monoliths don’t scale” sounds like you’re simply following trends.

8. Sidecar and service mesh

“When would you add a service mesh & what does it cost you?”

A service mesh is a layer of proxies, one beside each service, which handles all traffic between services.

Each proxy, called a sidecar, runs in the same pod as its service. Every request in and out passes through it. The sidecar handles encryption, retries, timeouts, and metrics. A control plane pushes rules to every sidecar at once.

You change a retry policy in one place, and the entire fleet follows.

  • It gives you encryption, retries, timeouts, and traffic metrics without code changes.

  • A service mesh becomes more useful when you have many microservices built with different programming languages.

  • But it adds extra delay on every call, extra memory in every pod, and makes the system complex.

  • Plus, debugging gets harder because a failure could occur in the proxy…not the service.

“How is a service mesh different from an API gateway?”

A gateway handles traffic coming into the system from clients…A mesh handles traffic between services inside the system.

Many large systems run both.

Adding a mesh to five services because it’s popular.

At that size, a library like Resilience4j covers retries and timeouts. Interviewers want to hear you weigh the running costs.

“Checkout request is slow & it touches ten services. How do you find the cause?”

Observability is your ability to understand a system’s inner state from logs, metrics, and traces it produces.

Logs record single events, like an error with its details. Metrics track numbers over time, like request rate and error rate. Traces follow one request across every service it touches.

Each service passes a shared trace ID along with the call. Your tracing tool then stitches the pieces into one timeline.

  • Start with a distributed trace. It shows how much time each service spent on the request.

  • Use metrics to spot which service’s latency or error rate went up.

  • Search the logs by trace ID to see the exact error.

  • Alert on what users feel, such as slow checkouts, not on every server metric.

“Tracing every request costs too much. What do you do?”

Sample. Keep a small share of normal traces and keep every trace with an error or a slow response. Set retention limits on logs as well.

Answering “I’d check the logs.”

Logs from ten services can’t be joined without a shared trace ID. Name tracing first.

10. Service-oriented architecture

“How is service-oriented architecture different from microservices?”

Service-oriented architecture () builds an application from large, shared services connected through a central messaging layer.

In SOA, one service covers an entire business function, like billing. Several applications reuse the same service. An enterprise service bus () sits in the middle. It routes messages, converts formats, and applies rules between services.

  • Size: SOA services are large and shared across applications. Microservices are small and built around one capability.

  • Logic: SOA puts routing and rules in the bus. Microservices keep the pipes simple and put logic inside each service.

  • Data: SOA services share a database. Each microservice owns its own data.

  • Releases: Shared SOA service needs sign-off from every consumer. A microservice ships on its own.

“Isn’t an API gateway just an enterprise service bus again?”

Only if you let it grow into one.

A gateway should route, check tokens, and apply rate limits. Once it starts holding business rules or joining data from many services, it becomes the bottleneck the bus was.

Watch for gateway changes in every feature release.

Saying “microservices are just SOA done right” without naming a single difference. Interviewers want concrete points. The bus and data ownership are the two clearest ones.

“How would you split an online shop’s monolith into services?”

A is a boundary inside which one domain model and its terms have one exact meaning.

Take the word “customer.” Sales sees a customer as a lead with a deal value. Support sees someone with open tickets. Shipping only needs a name and an address.

A bounded context lets each area keep its own small model instead of sharing one giant one.

  • Start from the business domain, not from database tables or code layers.

  • Find boundaries where words change meaning, such as “customer” or “product.”

  • Each context owns its model & data, and becomes a candidate service.

  • Map how contexts depend on each other, and which events pass between them.

  • Start with a few large contexts, and split further only when you have a reason.

“Two contexts both need customer data. Where does it live?”

One context owns the source of truth, such as customer service. It publishes an event whenever a customer changes. Other contexts keep their own copy with only the fields they need, updated from those events.

Splitting by technical layer, with one service for the user interface, one for logic, and one for data. Every feature then touches all three, so nothing ships alone. One service per database table fails the same way.

“Design rate limiting for a public API running on ten gateway instances.”

Rate limiting caps the number of requests a caller make in a set time window.

The gateway counts requests per user, API key, or IP address. Once a caller passes the limit, extra requests get an response. A common method is the token bucket.

Each caller has a bucket that refills at a steady rate & each request spends one token.

  • Limit per user or API key, not just per IP address.

  • Pick an algorithm: token bucket allows short bursts; sliding window gives smoother limits.

  • Also keep counters in a shared store like Redis, so all ten instances see the same count.

  • Return a with a header on limit.

  • Plus, set different limits per plan and per endpoint.

“Redis goes down. Do you block all traffic or let it through?”

Usually let it through, using rough limits inside each gateway instance.

An outage in the limiter then doesn’t become an outage of the entire API. For sensitive endpoints like login, block instead.

Counting inside each instance only. With ten instances, the real limit becomes ten times higher. Fixed time windows have a similar flaw since a caller can send double the limit on a window edge.

“Design a REST API for orders.”

Representational state transfer () is an API style where clients act on resources using standard HTTP methods.

A uniform resource locator () like names one order. GET reads it, POST creates one, PUT replaces it, and DELETE removes it. Responses normally come back as JSON.

Each request carries everything the server needs, so servers keep no session state between calls.

  • Use nouns for resources, such as and .

  • Use the right methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

  • Return clear status codes, such as for created, for not found, and for a conflict.

  • Paginate lists, and plan how you’ll version the API.

“A client retries POST after a timeout. How do you avoid creating two orders?”

Ask the client to send an idempotency key with each POST. The server stores the key with the result. A repeat request with the same key returns the stored result instead of creating a new order.

Putting verbs in URLs, like , or returning for every error with the real problem hidden in the body.

What happens next is up to you. Because the next time an interviewer asks you to design a microservices system, the answer won’t come from this letter. It’ll come from what you’ve learned and practiced.
